pairs.rationale: Both introduce Jesus teaching disciples in the presence of a crowd before the beatitudes. The settings differ: Matthew has Jesus ascend and sit on the mountain, whereas Luke has Him descend to a level place; the comparison does not erase that difference.
Matthew introduces Jesus addressing the disciples and then beginning the beatitudes; Luke likewise directs His gaze and opening blessing toward His disciples.
Both pronounce the poor blessed and promise them the kingdom. Matthew specifies poor in spirit and kingdom of the heavens, while Luke addresses the poor and names God's kingdom.
Matthew promises comfort to mourners; Luke promises future laughter to those who weep now. Both blessings reverse present sorrow without using identical wording.
The promise that the meek will inherit the earth closely recalls the psalm's promise that the meek will inherit the land and delight in peace. The target is Greek-numbered Psalm 36 in this edition.
Both bless those who hunger and promise that they will be filled. Matthew explicitly makes righteousness the object of hunger and adds thirst; Luke speaks of those who hunger now.
Matthew connects showing mercy with receiving mercy; James warns that judgment is without mercy for the person who has shown none and says mercy triumphs over judgment.

Matthew associates purity of heart with seeing God; the psalm describes the person with clean hands and a pure heart as qualified to stand in the Lord's holy place. This is a shared association between inward purity and access to God, not an identical promise.

Matthew blesses peacemakers and calls them God's sons; James describes a harvest of righteousness sown in peace for those who make peace. The common subject is active peacemaking; James does not repeat the sonship promise.
Both passages pronounce people blessed when they suffer for righteousness. Matthew adds the kingdom promise, while Peter tells the sufferers not to fear.

Both bless disciples who are reviled and socially rejected because of their association with Jesus. Matthew emphasizes false evil accusations for His sake; Luke speaks of hatred and exclusion because of the Son of Man.
Both command joy amid persecution, promise a great heavenly reward, and compare the disciples' treatment with the persecution of earlier prophets.

Both use salt that has lost its taste to describe something that can no longer serve its purpose and is thrown away. Matthew adds the disciples' identity as the earth's salt and the image of trampling.

Matthew calls the disciples the world's light; Paul describes believers shining as lights in the world amid a crooked generation. Philippians shares the public witness image without repeating Matthew's hilltop city.
Both say a lit lamp belongs on a lampstand rather than under a modius so that people may see its light. The household lamp supplies the same illustration in each teaching.
Both connect visible good works with other people glorifying God. Matthew tells disciples to let their light shine, while Peter applies good conduct to a setting where outsiders slander believers.

Jesus denies abolishing the Law and Prophets and speaks of fulfillment; Paul likewise denies that faith nullifies law and says it establishes law. The comparison concerns refusal to discard the law, without treating the two arguments as identical.
Both contrast the passing of heaven and earth with the enduring smallest written detail of the Law. Luke's small stroke corresponds to Matthew's iota and stroke.
Matthew warns against loosening even a least commandment; James says stumbling in one point makes a person accountable for the whole law. Both resist treating part of God's law as dispensable.

The later denunciation explains a concrete defect in the scribes' and Pharisees' righteousness: an outwardly righteous appearance can conceal hypocrisy and lawlessness. It helps illuminate the demand for righteousness exceeding theirs without equating every member of those groups with the criticism.
The command not to murder repeats the Decalogue prohibition. In this Saints Greek-based inventory it is Exodus 20:15; the command itself does not include Matthew's following judicial explanation.
Matthew brings anger toward a brother under judgment; John calls hatred of a brother murder. Both extend concern beyond the outward act of homicide to the inward hostility behind it.

Both bring damaged relationships into the setting of worship. Matthew asks the offerer to remember a brother's grievance, while Mark tells a praying person to forgive his own grievance against another; the directions of the grievance differ.

Matthew requires the worshiper first to seek reconciliation with his brother; Paul tells believers, as far as it depends on them, to live at peace with everyone. Both demand active efforts toward peaceful relationships.
Both urge reaching a settlement with an adversary while still on the way, before the adversary hands the debtor to a judge and officer and imprisonment follows.
Both conclude the adversary-and-prison saying by warning that release will wait until the smallest outstanding coin is paid. Matthew names a quadrans and Luke a lepton.
The prohibition of adultery repeats the Decalogue command. This Saints Greek-based edition places it at Exodus 20:13, rather than silently adopting another ordering of the commandments.

Matthew condemns a lustful look as inward adultery; Job describes a covenant governing his eyes so that he will not direct his attention toward a virgin. Both connect sexual integrity with disciplined looking, though Job does not formulate Matthew's judgment of the heart.
Both use the severe image of discarding an eye that causes stumbling and contrast losing one member with being thrown into Gehenna. Mark continues with the description of undying worm and fire.

Both use cutting off a hand that causes stumbling to stress the greater danger of Gehenna. Matthew contrasts the loss of one member with the whole body; Mark contrasts entering life maimed with retaining two hands.

Matthew's saying about giving a certificate of divorce recalls the certificate in Deuteronomy's case law. Deuteronomy describes the written certificate within a legal case; this comparison does not turn that description into an unrestricted command to divorce.

Both connect divorce and remarriage with adultery and specifically mention marrying a divorced woman. Matthew includes a sexual-immorality qualification and the husband's responsibility for causing adultery; Luke's wording here contains neither qualification.
Matthew's prohibition of swearing falsely recalls Leviticus's ban on swearing by God's name for an unjust cause and profaning His name. The shared concern is misuse of an oath invoking God.

Matthew's instruction to fulfill oaths to the Lord corresponds to Deuteronomy's requirement not to delay paying a vow and to do what has proceeded from one's lips. Deuteronomy also distinguishes a voluntarily unmade vow from a vow that binds its maker.

Jesus explains that heaven must not be used as an oath object because it is God's throne; Isaiah explicitly calls heaven the Lord's throne. The throne image supplies the stated reason, while Isaiah is not itself an oath prohibition.
Matthew's description of earth as the footstool of God's feet closely recalls Isaiah's description of earth as His footstool. Jesus applies the image to the prohibition on swearing by the earth.
The designation of Jerusalem as the city of the great King recalls the psalm's description of Zion as the city of the great King. The target retains this edition's Greek numbering, Psalm 47:3.

Matthew forbids swearing by one's head and gives human inability to control even one hair's color as a reason; James forbids any other oath in addition to heaven and earth. The general oath prohibition corresponds, though James does not repeat the hair illustration.
Both replace oath-taking with a dependable yes and no. James repeats the paired yes and no and connects the instruction with avoiding judgment.
Matthew's eye-for-eye and tooth-for-tooth formula repeats the matching clauses in Exodus's legal rule of corresponding injury. The target also continues the series with hand and foot.
Both instruct a person struck on one cheek to offer the other. Matthew places the instruction under not resisting the evildoer and specifies the right cheek.

Both pair tunic and cloak in an instruction to surrender more than an opponent takes. Matthew begins with a lawsuit over the tunic and adds the cloak; Luke begins with the cloak and says not to withhold the tunic.
Both tell disciples to give to the person who asks. Matthew adds not turning away a prospective borrower; Luke adds not demanding possessions back from someone who takes them.

The love-your-neighbor portion recalls Leviticus's command to love the neighbor as oneself. Leviticus also forbids vengeance and lingering anger; it does not supply Matthew's accompanying hate-your-enemy clause.
Both command love for enemies and prayer for those who mistreat the disciples. Luke also specifies doing good to haters and blessing those who curse.

Both connect loving enemies with becoming children of God and ground that conduct in God's kindness toward evil people. Matthew illustrates indiscriminate beneficence with sunshine and rain; Luke mentions kindness to the ungrateful and evil.

Both ask what reward or credit there is in loving only those who return love, since people outside the disciples' community also do that. Matthew uses tax collectors as the comparison; Luke uses sinners.

Both challenge conduct limited to reciprocating ordinary social goodwill. Matthew's example is greeting only brothers, while Luke's is doing good only to those who do good in return; these are corresponding arguments with different examples.
Both end the enemy-love teaching by calling disciples to model their conduct on their Father. Matthew uses perfect and Luke uses merciful; the wording and emphasis remain distinct.

The later criticism that religious leaders do their works to be seen by people directly parallels the warning against practicing righteousness for the purpose of being seen. Matthew 6 adds the consequence of losing the Father's reward.
Both connect giving to the poor with repayment. Proverbs names God as the one who repays the gift; Matthew warns that public praise can become the ostentatious giver's entire reward.

Matthew promises the Father's repayment for alms given in secret; Proverbs says the giver who has mercy on the poor lends to God and will be repaid by Him. The shared point is divine repayment, while secrecy is specific to Matthew.

Matthew 6 criticizes prayers staged for public visibility in synagogues and streets; the later passage criticizes works performed to be seen and love of prominent synagogue seats. Both expose religious conduct arranged for public honor.

Jesus instructs a person to shut the door and pray privately; Elisha is narrated entering the house, shutting the door behind himself and the child, and praying to the Lord. The shared action illustrates secluded prayer without making Elisha's emergency identical to the command's setting.

Matthew rejects the idea that many words secure a hearing from God; Ecclesiastes urges few words before God and associates a fool's voice with many words. Both caution against unrestrained religious speech.
Both ground trust in the Father in His prior knowledge of human needs. Matthew applies that knowledge to prayer; Luke applies it to seeking food and drink.
Both model prayer by addressing the Father and asking that His name be hallowed. Matthew expands the address to our Father in the heavens.
Both prayers ask for the coming of God's kingdom. Matthew also asks that God's will be done on earth as in heaven; that additional petition is absent from this verse of Luke's supplied text.
Both model a petition for daily bread. Matthew says this day, while Luke says day by day.
Both connect the petition for divine forgiveness with forgiving others. Matthew speaks of debts and debtors; Luke asks forgiveness of sins while retaining the language of what others owe.

Both prayers ask not to be brought into temptation or testing. Matthew continues with deliverance from evil; Luke's supplied wording ends with the testing petition and does not include that additional clause.
Both connect forgiving other people with the heavenly Father's forgiveness of the worshiper's trespasses. Mark places the instruction within standing prayer.

Matthew states negatively the condition that Mark expresses positively: refusing to forgive others is incompatible with receiving the Father's forgiveness of one's own trespasses. Mark does not separately repeat Matthew's negative sentence.

Matthew rejects conspicuously miserable fasting staged for human recognition; Isaiah rejects the assumption that bowed posture, sackcloth, and ashes by themselves constitute an acceptable fast. Both challenge outward displays of fasting, though Isaiah's passage focuses on the fast God chooses.
This explicitly same-chapter comparison repeats the promise of repayment by the Father who sees in secret: Matthew 6:4 applies it to almsgiving, while 6:18 applies it to fasting.

Matthew warns against earthly treasure vulnerable to moth and theft; Luke urges an unfailing heavenly treasure where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. Both contrast fragile possessions with secure heavenly treasure.
Both command the accumulation of heavenly treasure protected from thieves and moths. Luke connects that instruction with selling possessions and giving alms.
Both give the same reason for choosing one's treasure carefully: the heart will be where the treasure is.
Both call the eye the lamp of the body and connect a sound or single eye with the whole body being full of light.

Both contrast an evil eye and bodily darkness with true light, and warn that what seems to be light within a person can be darkness. Matthew intensifies the warning with the question about how great that darkness is.
Both use slavery to two masters to illustrate incompatible allegiance: love and loyalty to one oppose love and loyalty to the other, so a person cannot serve God and mammon together.
Both tell disciples not to be anxious about food or clothing and reason that life is more than food and the body more than clothing. Matthew includes drinking among the immediate concerns.
Both point to birds that neither sow nor reap nor store food, yet are fed by God, and argue that the disciples are worth more. Luke names ravens, while Matthew refers to birds of the sky.
Both ask whether anxiety can add a cubit to a person's span of life. The unusual cubit image is preserved in both supplied texts.
Both direct attention to lilies that do not toil or spin as an answer to anxiety about clothing. Luke also includes the following comparison with Solomon within the same verse.
Both say that even Solomon in all his glory was not clothed like one of the lilies. Matthew places the Solomon comparison in a verse after the instruction to observe their growth.
Both reason from God's clothing of grass that exists today and is thrown into an oven tomorrow to His greater care for people, and both address their lack of faith.
Both tell the disciples not to be preoccupied with what they will eat or drink. Matthew includes the anxious question about clothing as well.
Both contrast the nations' pursuit of daily necessities with the Father's knowledge that the disciples need those things.
Both redirect the pursuit of necessities toward seeking God's kingdom and promise that these things will be added. Matthew explicitly includes seeking His righteousness.

Both warn about one's attitude toward tomorrow. Matthew rejects anxiety and says the present day has sufficient trouble; Proverbs rejects boasting about tomorrow because the coming day's events are unknown. This is a limited thematic comparison between different responses to the future, not an equation of anxiety with boasting.
Both forbid judging and link refraining from judgment with not being judged. Luke continues with condemnation and release.
Both say that the measure people use will be measured back to them. Matthew applies the principle to judgment, while Luke places it in an instruction about giving.
Both ask why someone sees a small splinter or speck in a brother's eye while failing to notice the beam in his own eye.
Both expose the absurdity of offering to remove a brother's speck while the helper still has a beam in his own eye. Luke joins the question and the remedy within one verse.
Both address the would-be corrector as a hypocrite and require removal of one's own beam before one can see clearly to remove a brother's speck.

Compare the warning about offering holy and valuable things to recipients who respond destructively with the warning against speaking intelligent words to a fool who will sneer. This is a thematic comparison about discernment, not an identification of Matthew's symbolic animals with every foolish person.
Both present the three commands ask, seek, and knock, each joined to its corresponding promise of receiving, finding, and an opened door.
Both explain the preceding commands by saying that the one who asks receives, the seeker finds, and the door is opened to the one who knocks.

Both use a father's response to a child's request for food to show the incongruity of giving something harmful instead. Matthew's example is bread and a stone; Luke's supplied text uses fish and snake, then egg and scorpion, and does not repeat the bread example.
Both ask whether a father would replace the fish requested by his son with a snake. The shared food-and-danger contrast supports the following argument about the Father.
Both reason from the good gifts given by imperfect human parents to the heavenly Father's greater generosity. Matthew promises good things to those who ask; Luke specifically names the Holy Spirit.
Both command people to treat others as they themselves wish to be treated. Matthew additionally identifies this instruction with the Law and the Prophets.

Both urge entry through a narrow opening. Matthew contrasts that instruction with the broad road to destruction that many enter; Luke warns that many will seek to enter the narrow door without being able. The exhortations correspond, while their descriptions of the many differ.

Matthew describes the narrow gate and constricted road to life as found by few; Luke urges striving to enter the narrow door because many will seek entry without being able. The narrow-entry warning corresponds without identifying all details of gate, road, and door.

Both warn the believing community about dangerous teachers pictured as wolves. Matthew describes false prophets disguised as sheep; Paul warns of wolves entering the flock and men using distorted speech to draw disciples after themselves.
Both use a tree's fruit as the means of recognizing its character and illustrate the point with the impossibility of harvesting figs or grapes from thorny plants.
Both contrast a good tree with a rotten tree by the kind of fruit each produces. Matthew states what each bears; Luke states what each cannot produce.
Both deny that a good tree produces evil or rotten fruit, or that a rotten tree produces good fruit. The fruit image supplies a test of the underlying source.
Matthew repeats the warning found in John's preaching in Luke: every tree that does not produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into fire.

Matthew concludes that the false prophets will be recognized by their fruits; Luke states the general image that every tree is known by its own fruit. The connection is the same fruit-based criterion of recognition.
Both deny that addressing Jesus as Lord is sufficient when obedience is absent. Matthew requires doing the Father's will; Luke asks why people say Lord, Lord while failing to do what He says.

Matthew depicts people appealing to prophecy and mighty works as evidence of standing with Jesus; Paul says that even prophecy and mountain-moving faith amount to nothing without love. Both challenge reliance on extraordinary religious gifts alone, though Paul does not repeat the judgment scene or the claim about exorcisms.

Both portray a decisive refusal of people who claim association with the Lord, followed by a command that workers of wrongdoing depart. Matthew says I never knew you; Luke says I do not know you or where you come from.

The command for workers of lawlessness to depart recalls the psalmist's command that all workers of lawlessness stand away from him. Matthew places the declaration on Jesus' lips in the judgment scene; this edition numbers the target Psalm 6:9.
Both compare a person who hears Jesus' words and acts on them to a builder who establishes a house on rock. Luke adds the detail of digging deeply for the foundation.
Both describe a house remaining secure when a flood or river strikes because it has been properly founded. Matthew includes rain and wind and explicitly repeats that the foundation was rock.
Both compare hearing without acting to an unsound house. Matthew has a foolish builder on sand; Luke describes a house built on the ground without a foundation.
Both conclude that the house corresponding to hearing without obedience collapses when the river strikes, and both emphasize how great its ruin is. Matthew also lists rain and wind.
Both narrate the audience's astonishment at Jesus' teaching. Matthew reports it after the completed sermon; Mark reports it in the Capernaum synagogue setting.
Both explain astonishment by contrasting Jesus' teaching with that of the scribes: He teaches as one having authority. The common evaluation is retained while the narrative occasions differ.

deferred.reason: The distinctive instruction to go a second Roman mile after compulsory service was read. General teachings about doing good amid mistreatment were considered, but no sufficiently close independently supported passage was retained in this initial batch.

The instruction not to let the left hand know the right hand's almsgiving was read. No separate passage with a sufficiently precise correspondence to this distinctive secrecy image was retained; neighboring teaching was not used merely to manufacture a completion.

The concrete instructions to anoint the head and wash the face while fasting were read. General passages about inward fasting were reviewed, but none was retained as a sufficiently precise counterpart to these particular actions.

review_notes: All 111 source verse units in Matthew 5–7 were read from the supplied Saints English records. Source wording is unchanged; this file contains editorial proposals only.
Target passages were read from the supplied reference records; Exodus quotation targets were checked again against cache-exact/exodus.json after the parent identified an older cache copy.

Greek-based Saints numbering is retained: Exodus 20:15 is the murder command, Exodus 20:13 the adultery command, Psalm 36:11 the meek inheritance promise, Psalm 47:3 the city of the great King, and Psalm 6:9 the departure of lawless workers.

Parallels between Matthew and Luke preserve substantive differences, including poor in spirit versus poor; perfection versus mercy; the different petitions in the supplied Lord's Prayer texts; and different examples of parental gifts.
Leviticus 19:18 supports the love-your-neighbor clause in Matthew 5:43 and does not support the accompanying hate-your-enemy clause.
The Matthew 6:18 to 6:4 link is explicitly a same-chapter repeated formula. Other Matthew targets are in separate chapters.
Review is AI-assisted English passage comparison, not an exhaustive concordance, a fresh Greek critical-text review, or independent specialist approval.
